# Introduction
`scMaSigPro` is designed to handle datasets with at least two branches and
requires that cells be assigned exclusively to these branches. This vignette
demonstrates how to evaluate datasets with common root cells using the `scMaSigPro`
approach. We use a simulated multifurcating trajectory that was analysed with
Monocle3 and is bundled with the package as a `SingleCellExperiment` object
(`multi.lin.sce`), so everything below runs offline.

## Installation

Currently, `scMaSigPro` is available on GitHub and can be installed as follows:

```{r, "install", eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
# Install BiocManager if needed, then scMaSigPro together with its
# Bioconductor dependencies from GitHub
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("BioBam/scMaSigPro")
```

## Setup
We will start by loading the necessary libraries.
```{r, "libs", message=FALSE}
library(scMaSigPro)
library(ggplot2)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
```

## Simulated Data
For this vignette, we use a simulated dataset containing 1,977 cells and 501
genes. The dataset was generated using the Dyntoy package and is sourced from
the [`tradeSeq` repository](https://github.com/statOmics/tradeSeqPaper/raw/master/simulation/sim2_dyntoy_multifurcating_4/multifurcating_4.rds).
It was simulated to have three branches and analysed with Monocle3
(version 1.3.4): a principal graph was learned on a t-SNE embedding, pseudotime
was inferred from the root node, and every cell was assigned to a branch of the
graph. The result is bundled as `multi.lin.sce`; see `?multi.lin.sce` and
`system.file("scripts", "make-multi-lin-sce.R", package = "scMaSigPro")` for
the exact code that produced it.

```{r, "load-data"}
data("multi.lin.sce", package = "scMaSigPro")
multi.lin.sce
head(colData(multi.lin.sce), 3)
```

The `colData` holds the two columns `scMaSigPro` needs: `group`, the hard
assignment of each cell to a branch of the trajectory, and
`Monocle3_Pseudotime`.

```{r, "plot-tsne", fig.align='center', fig.width=10, fig.height=5, fig.alt='t-SNE of the multifurcating trajectory coloured by branch assignment (A) and by Monocle3 pseudotime (B)'}
tsne <- as.data.frame(reducedDim(multi.lin.sce, "TSNE"))
colnames(tsne) <- c("tSNE1", "tSNE2")
tsne$group <- colData(multi.lin.sce)$group
tsne$pseudotime <- colData(multi.lin.sce)$Monocle3_Pseudotime

p_group <- ggplot(tsne, aes(x = tSNE1, y = tSNE2, colour = group)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.7, alpha = 0.8) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
    labs(title = "A. Branch assignment", colour = "Branch")

p_time <- ggplot(tsne, aes(x = tSNE1, y = tSNE2, colour = pseudotime)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.7, alpha = 0.8) +
    scale_colour_viridis_c() +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
    labs(title = "B. Monocle3 pseudotime", colour = "Pseudotime")

patchwork::wrap_plots(p_group, p_time, ncol = 2)
```

In panel A, the cells share a common root (`root`) and then diverge. One branch
leads directly to the endpoint `path_Y_52`. The other continues as a segment
shared by two later branches (labelled `path_Y_18|path_Y_15`, the *link*)
before splitting into `path_Y_15` and `path_Y_18`. Panel B shows the universal
Monocle3 pseudotime that all branches share. These five elements (root, link
and three branches) are the input for the common-root-cells setup.

## Hard Assignment of Cells
An important prerequisite for using `scMaSigPro` is the hard assignment of cells
to branches. This means that each cell must be exclusively assigned to one branch.
There are broadly two ways to assign cells:

1. Hard assignment (0 and 1), where each cell belongs to only one branch.
2. Soft assignment (0 to 1), where a cell can belong to multiple branches simultaneously.

In Monocle3, each cell is associated with only one branch, implying a hard assignment,
which is suitable for `scMaSigPro` current version. On the other hand, `tradeSeq` can
handle both hard and soft assignments. In Slingshot, for instance, cells can be
part of multiple branches, which is a form of soft assignment. One key difference
is that Slingshot assigns different pseudotimes to each branch, whereas Monocle3
uses a universal pseudotime for all branches.

## Extracting Assignments from Monocle3
The `group` column of `multi.lin.sce` was derived from the Monocle3 object by
following the steps of the [`tradeSeq` vignette](https://statomics.github.io/tradeSeq/articles/Monocle.html#extracting-the-pseudotimes-and-cell-weights-for-tradeseq-1):
for every endpoint of the principal graph, find the shortest path back to the
root; a cell belongs to a path when its closest principal node lies on it. A
cell on all three paths is a root cell, a cell on exactly two paths is a link
cell, and a cell on one path belongs to that branch. The recipe below shows how
to do this on your own `cell_data_set`; it is not evaluated here because
Monocle3 is not a dependency of `scMaSigPro`.

```{r, "monocle3-recipe", eval=FALSE}
## Requires monocle3 and a `cds` with a learned graph and ordered cells.
## `cds` here had t-SNE coordinates stored in the UMAP slot, because
## monocle3::learn_graph() only works on the UMAP slot (monocle3 issue #242).
y_to_cells <- as.data.frame(
    principal_graph_aux(cds)$UMAP$pr_graph_cell_proj_closest_vertex
)
y_to_cells$cells <- rownames(y_to_cells)
y_to_cells$Y <- y_to_cells$V1

root <- principal_graph_aux(cds)$UMAP$root_pr_nodes
mst <- principal_graph(cds)$UMAP
endpoints <- names(which(igraph::degree(mst) == 1))
endpoints <- endpoints[!endpoints %in% root]

cellWeights <- lapply(endpoints, function(endpoint) {
    path <- igraph::shortest_paths(mst, root, endpoint)$vpath[[1]]
    path <- as.character(path)
    df <- y_to_cells[y_to_cells$Y %in% path, ]
    df <- data.frame(weights = as.numeric(colnames(cds) %in% df$cells))
    colnames(df) <- endpoint
    df
})
cellWeights <- as.matrix(do.call(cbind, cellWeights))
rownames(cellWeights) <- colnames(cds)
colnames(cellWeights) <- paste("path", colnames(cellWeights), sep = "_")

# Keep three endpoints and the cells that lie on at least one of their paths
cellWeights <- cellWeights[, c("path_Y_18", "path_Y_52", "path_Y_15")]
cellWeights <- cellWeights[rowSums(cellWeights) != 0, ]

group <- apply(cellWeights, 1, function(x) {
    on <- names(x)[x == 1]
    if (length(on) == 3) "root" else paste(on, collapse = "|")
})

# Cell table with the Monocle3 pseudotime and the path label of each kept
# cell; it holds the same information as colData(multi.lin.sce) used below
cell_data <- data.frame(
    Pseudotime = pseudotime(cds)[names(group)],
    Path = group,
    row.names = names(group)
)
```

## `scMaSigPro` object
We take the cell metadata from the bundled object and shorten the branch
labels: the `path_` prefix is dropped, the shared segment is written as
`Y_18_links_Y_15` (the separator that `sc.restruct()` expects by default), and
the root is capitalised so that it sorts first and therefore becomes the
reference path of the model.

```{r, "cell-metadata"}
cellData <- as.data.frame(colData(multi.lin.sce))
cellData$group <- gsub("path_", "", cellData$group, fixed = TRUE)
cellData$group <- gsub("|", "_links_", cellData$group, fixed = TRUE)
# The alphabetically first label becomes the reference path. Capitalising
# "Root" keeps it first in every locale (uppercase sorts before lowercase in
# the C locale that R CMD build uses, and alphabetically elsewhere).
cellData$group[cellData$group == "root"] <- "Root"
table(cellData$group)
```

If a cell belongs to the root, it is part of all the paths. If a cell is part
of the link segment, it is part of both the `Y_15` and `Y_18` branches.

### Creating Object
```{r, "create-object"}
multi_scmp_ob <- create_scmp(
    counts = as.matrix(counts(multi.lin.sce)),
    cell_data = cellData,
    ptime_col = "Monocle3_Pseudotime",
    path_col = "group",
    use_as_bin = FALSE
)
multi_scmp_ob
```

# Each Branch as a Group (Approach-1)

The first approach to using `scMaSigPro` to analyze branches with common cells
is to consider the common cells as a separate group. For the interpretation we
will evaluate whether a particular gene's expression in the common root cells and
its downstream branch is similar.

## Perform Binning
```{r, "approach-1-binning", fig.align='center', fig.width=8, fig.height=5, fig.alt='Bin sizes per branch and binned pseudotime, each branch as a group'}
## Pseudotime based binning
multi_scmp_ob_A <- sc.squeeze(multi_scmp_ob)

## Plot bin information
plotBinTile(multi_scmp_ob_A)
```

In the above figure, we can see that `scMaSigPro` considers each group as a
separate branch. Running `scMaSigPro` with this configuration will lead to a
different interpretation of the data. This will help us evaluate whether the
expression changes across branches compared to root. If you want to consider
the common root cells and branches together, you can follow the next section.

Additionally, we can see that the common root cells and the resulting branches
have the same values of binned pseudotime values. This is because the binning
is performed independently over each branch.

## Running Workflow
```{r, "approach-1-workflow", fig.align='center', fig.width=8, fig.height=5, fig.alt='Upset plot of significant genes per branch, each branch as a group'}
# Polynomial Degree 3
multi_scmp_ob_A <- sc.set.poly(multi_scmp_ob_A, poly_degree = 3)

# Detect non-flat profiles
multi_scmp_ob_A <- sc.p.vector(
    multi_scmp_ob_A,
    verbose = FALSE
)

# Model refinement
multi_scmp_ob_A <- sc.t.fit(
    multi_scmp_ob_A,
    verbose = FALSE
)

# Apply filter
multi_scmp_ob_A <- sc.filter(
    scmpObj = multi_scmp_ob_A,
    rsq = 0.55,
    vars = "groups",
    intercept = "dummy",
    includeInflu = TRUE
)

# Plot upset
plotIntersect(multi_scmp_ob_A)
```

`scMaSigPro` treated `Root` as the reference for all branches. Starting
from `scMaSigPro` version `0.0.4`, `plotIntersect(return = TRUE)` returns the
intersection information as a data frame, with one column per gene set.

## Significant Genes
```{r, "extract-intersection"}
shared_genes <- plotIntersect(multi_scmp_ob_A, return = TRUE)
head(shared_genes)
n_shared <- sum(rowSums(shared_genes) == ncol(shared_genes))
```

In the upset plot above, we can see that there are `r n_shared` genes which
change among all branches and also change with pseudotime. We will explore them
later. First, let's look at the genes that have similar expression in the
`Root`, the link segment and the `Y_15` branch: those genes are significant for
`Y_52vsRoot` and `Y_18vsRoot` but not for `Y_18_links_Y_15vsRoot` or
`Y_15vsRoot`.

```{r, "sample-gene", fig.align='center', fig.width=8, fig.height=5, fig.alt='Trend of one gene with similar expression in root, link and Y_15'}
## Similar expression in Root, the link segment and Y_15
gene_br_Y_15 <- rownames(shared_genes)[
    shared_genes$Y_52vsRoot == 1 &
        shared_genes$Y_18vsRoot == 1 &
        shared_genes$Y_15vsRoot == 0 &
        shared_genes$Root == 1 &
        shared_genes$Y_18_links_Y_15vsRoot == 0
]
head(gene_br_Y_15)
plotTrend(multi_scmp_ob_A, feature_id = gene_br_Y_15[1], points = FALSE, lines = TRUE)
```

In the above plot, we can see that the gene `r gene_br_Y_15[1]` has a similar
expression in `Root`, the link segment and `Y_15`. This is a good example
of how `scMaSigPro` can be used to identify genes that show similar patterns in
the common root cells and how different they are in other branches. The main
idea is to set the root as a reference and then compare the branches to the root.

Next we can explore the `r n_shared` genes that we have in the intersection. As
it is hard to see them all at once, we will first perform clustering and then
look at them in groups.

```{r, "approach-1-clusters", fig.align='center', fig.width=8, fig.height=5, fig.alt='Clustered gene trends, each branch as a group'}
## Perform Clustering
multi_scmp_ob_A <- sc.cluster.trend(multi_scmp_ob_A)

# Plot Clusters
plotTrendCluster(multi_scmp_ob_A, verbose = FALSE, loess_span = 0.8)
```

# Ordering Common Cells (Approach-2)

Another approach is to reorder the pseudotime bins, meaning the bins representing
the common root cells are ordered first, followed by the bins of the branches.
This helps compare the gene expression of the common root cells together with the
downstream branches.

## Reorder Bins Manually

### Extract Binned Data
```{r, "extract-binned-data"}
binned_data <- cDense(multi_scmp_ob_A)
head(binned_data[, -2])
```

### Create Bin Data for Root + Y_52
The main idea is to update the values in the binned pseudotime column using an
offset. Based on our dataset, we observe that Y_52 is a branch that directly
originated from the Root. Therefore, the bins of the Y_52 branch should be aligned
right after it. This means that the offset for the Y_52 branch will be the maximum
value of the binned pseudotime of the root branch.

```{r, "bins-root-y52"}
## Create a new df
Y_52_binned_data <- binned_data[binned_data$group %in% c("Root", "Y_52"), , drop = FALSE]

## Calculate Offset (Max Value of the root)
Y_52_offset <- max(Y_52_binned_data[Y_52_binned_data$group == "Root", "scmp_binned_pseudotime"])

## Add offset
Y_52_binned_data[Y_52_binned_data$group == "Y_52", "scmp_binned_pseudotime"] <- Y_52_binned_data[Y_52_binned_data$group == "Y_52", "scmp_binned_pseudotime"] + Y_52_offset

## Update bins and rownames
Y_52_binned_data$group2 <- "Y_52"
rownames(Y_52_binned_data) <- paste(Y_52_binned_data$group2, Y_52_binned_data$scmp_binned_pseudotime, sep = "_bin_")

head(Y_52_binned_data[, -2])
```

### Create Bin Data for Root + Link + Y_15|Y_18
For the other branches we will add an offset of both "link" and "Y_15|Y_18".
```{r, "bins-root-link-y15-y18", fig.align='center', fig.width=8, fig.height=5, fig.alt='Original and shifted bins of branch Y_18'}
## Create a new df
Y_18_binned_data <- binned_data[binned_data$group %in% c("Root", "Y_18_links_Y_15", "Y_18"), , drop = FALSE]
Y_15_binned_data <- binned_data[binned_data$group %in% c("Root", "Y_18_links_Y_15", "Y_15"), , drop = FALSE]

## Calculate Offset (Max Value of the root and Link)
Y_18_root_offset <- max(Y_18_binned_data[Y_18_binned_data$group == "Root", "scmp_binned_pseudotime"])
Y_18_link_offset <- max(Y_18_binned_data[Y_18_binned_data$group == "Y_18_links_Y_15", "scmp_binned_pseudotime"])

## Add link offset to branch Y_18
Y_18_binned_data[Y_18_binned_data$group == "Y_18", "scmp_binned_pseudotime"] <- Y_18_binned_data[Y_18_binned_data$group == "Y_18", "scmp_binned_pseudotime"] + Y_18_link_offset
Y_15_binned_data[Y_15_binned_data$group == "Y_15", "scmp_binned_pseudotime"] <- Y_15_binned_data[Y_15_binned_data$group == "Y_15", "scmp_binned_pseudotime"] + Y_18_link_offset

## Add root offset to (link+ branch)
Y_18_binned_data[Y_18_binned_data$group != "Root", "scmp_binned_pseudotime"] <- Y_18_binned_data[Y_18_binned_data$group != "Root", "scmp_binned_pseudotime"] + Y_18_root_offset
Y_15_binned_data[Y_15_binned_data$group != "Root", "scmp_binned_pseudotime"] <- Y_15_binned_data[Y_15_binned_data$group != "Root", "scmp_binned_pseudotime"] + Y_18_root_offset

## Update bins and rownames
Y_18_binned_data$group2 <- "Y_18"
rownames(Y_18_binned_data) <- paste(Y_18_binned_data$group2, Y_18_binned_data$scmp_binned_pseudotime, sep = "_bin_")
Y_15_binned_data$group2 <- "Y_15"
rownames(Y_15_binned_data) <- paste(Y_15_binned_data$group2, Y_15_binned_data$scmp_binned_pseudotime, sep = "_bin_")

# Create plot
ggplot() +
    geom_tile(
        data = Y_18_binned_data,
        aes(x = scmp_binned_pseudotime, y = group), fill = "blue", alpha = 0.2
    ) +
    geom_tile(
        data = Y_18_binned_data,
        aes(x = scmp_binned_pseudotime, y = group2), fill = "red", alpha = 0.2
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
```

As we can see above, the tiles in blue represent the original bins, while the
red tiles represent the new bins of `Y_18`. At the end, we also observe the
overlap where the original bins of branch Y_18 are shifted to the end.

## Pseudobulk
```{r, "pseudobulk-manual", fig.align='center', fig.width=8, fig.height=5, fig.alt='Bin sizes after manual reordering'}
## Combine all metadata
new_binned_data <- rbind(Y_52_binned_data, Y_18_binned_data, Y_15_binned_data)

## Create a new object
multi_scmp_ob_A_manual <- multi_scmp_ob_A

## Update dense Metadata slot
cDense(multi_scmp_ob_A_manual) <- new_binned_data

## Set the group used for binning
multi_scmp_ob_A_manual@Parameters@path_col <- "group2"

## Perform Aggregation
multi_scmp_ob_A_manual <- pb_counts(
    scmpObj = multi_scmp_ob_A_manual,
    assay_name = "counts",
)

## Plot
plotBinTile(multi_scmp_ob_A_manual)
```

From `scMaSigPro` version `0.0.4` onwards, a wrapper function was introduced
to assist in ordering the bins. The working of the wrapper function `sc.restruct()`
is shown below, and it works on fairly simplified datasets like the one demonstrated
in this vignette.

## Reorder Bins with `sc.restruct()`
```{r, "restruct", fig.align='center', fig.width=8, fig.height=5, fig.alt='Bin sizes after reordering with sc.restruct()'}
## Showcase sc.restruct wrapper
multi_scmp_ob_B <- sc.restruct(multi_scmp_ob_A,
    end_node_list = list("Y_15", "Y_18", "Y_52"),
    root_node = "Root", link_node_list = list("Y_18_links_Y_15"),
    verbose = FALSE, link_sep = "_links_", assay_name = "counts", aggregate = "sum"
)
# Show the new path
plotBinTile(multi_scmp_ob_B)
```

As we see in the plot above, the `sc.restruct()` wrapper function performs the
exact transformations internally. For more complex trajectories, construct the
bin table manually as shown in the previous section.

## Running Workflow
```{r, "approach-2-workflow", fig.align='center', fig.width=8, fig.height=5, fig.alt='Upset plot of significant genes per branch after reordering'}
# Polynomial Degree 3
multi_scmp_ob_B <- sc.set.poly(multi_scmp_ob_B, poly_degree = 3)

# Detect non-flat profiles
multi_scmp_ob_B <- sc.p.vector(
    multi_scmp_ob_B,
    verbose = FALSE
)

# Model refinement
multi_scmp_ob_B <- sc.t.fit(
    multi_scmp_ob_B,
    verbose = FALSE
)

# Apply filter
multi_scmp_ob_B <- sc.filter(
    scmpObj = multi_scmp_ob_B,
    rsq = 0.5,
    vars = "groups",
    intercept = "dummy",
    includeInflu = TRUE
)

# Plot upset
plotIntersect(multi_scmp_ob_B)
```

Now, in the above scenario, Y_15 is treated as the reference, and we will look
at the genes that are expressed differently compared to this branch. This approach
will help us understand how genes are changing across the branches while considering
the root cells for each of the downstream branches.

## Significant Genes
```{r, "approach-2-clusters", fig.align='center', fig.width=8, fig.height=5, fig.alt='Clustered gene trends after reordering'}
## Perform Clustering
multi_scmp_ob_B <- sc.cluster.trend(multi_scmp_ob_B,
    k = 4, cluster_method = "kmeans"
)

## Plot Clusters
plotTrendCluster(multi_scmp_ob_B, verbose = FALSE)
```
